newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: FEATURE - Anarchy prompts rethinking of regional order.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Anarchy prompts rethinking of regional order.

text.p: Ethnic Albanian separatists in Macedonia and Serbia, shorn of their lifeline of support by the sudden collapse of Albania, are rethinking their relations with their host countries.

Diplomats say the chaos in Tirana has punctured the dream of a greater Albania, with parts of Macedonia and the southern Serbian province of Kosovo uniting with Albania, prompting a new mood of pragmatism among ethnic Albanian leaders.
The paradox is that Albania's tragedy could open the way to an era of stability elsewhere in the southern Balkans where ethnic Albanian ambitions have been viewed with alarm and hostility.
Albania was the essential source of moral, material and political support to its ethnic kin in neighbouring Macedonia and Yugoslavia.

"Now that the motherland is in an upheaval, I sincerely doubt anyone can find time to spare to bother with Kosovo for quite some time to come," Blerim Shala, an Albanian political analyst and journalist, told Reuters.
He foresaw an effort by the Kosovo Albanians to end the boycott of cooperation with Serbia and negotiate an agreement which would return them to the Yugoslav political fold.
Macedonia could also join a reorganised and democratic Yugoslav federation to ease its own ethnic tensions and boost internal and external stability, said Shala.
Such moves would help lessen the nationalist tensions which led to the bloody disintegration of former Yugoslavia in 1991 when four republics, including Macedonia, seceded.
SOLUTION COULD BE IN SIGHT FOR KOSOVO
Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic rescinded Kosovo's autonomy in 1989, claiming the Albanians wanted to secede to create a Greater Albania.

Albanian leaders do not conceal their ultimate goal is independent Kosovo although the province is sacred to Serbs and is recognised by the international community as being an integral part of Serbia.
To keep the lid on the province, where ethnic Albanians outnumber Serbs by nine to one, Milosevic has been forced to turn it into an army and police garrison which he can no longer afford.
The United States has offered him a powerful incentive to reach a political peace with ethnic Albanian leaders in the Kosovo capital of Pristina.

If he makes a deal, the United States would be much closer to lifting its veto on Serbia's return to international financial and diplomatic bodies and allowing Belgrade access to the foreign credits needed to rebuild its economy.
The Kosovo Albanians have reached a point where they must chose between abandoning their dreams of independence or radicalising their resistance.
"The Albanians now see their future in the restructuring of relations with Yugoslavia. Tirana's collapse has strengthened the hand of those willing to negotiate," a Western diplomat said.
Publicly, Serb nationalists in Kosovo oppose any compromise with the Albanians but most Serbs flinch from the risk of more violence after the wars that followed Croatian and Bosnian secession.
Privately Serbs admit that they could live even with a Kosovo Albanian republic as part of federal Yugoslavia but with no right to secede.
"Talk about changing borders is out of the question. The Albanian republic will have no rights to seceede," Shala said.
ETHNIC ALBANIANS PRESS FOR AUTONOMY IN MACEDONIA

In neighbouring Macedonia, where they officially make up 22 percent of the two million population, ethnic Albanians are pressing for autonomy and parallel institutions, including their own university.
The Albanian mayors of the towns of Tetovo and Gostivar say Albanians can no longer prosper in joint institutions with the Macedonians and must go their own way.
Analysts said Macedonia would have to reconsider its poor economic and strategic position between Albania to the west, Greece to the south and Bulgaria to the east.
"Yugoslavia to the north could be its best bet as a loose alliance of equal democratic states," the diplomat said.
Milosevic, Macedonian President Kiro Gligorov and Kosovo leader Ibrahim Rugova would benefit from ensuing stabilty.
Milosevic would head a strong, internationally recongised country with access to international financial institutions and western support.
Gligorov would avoid ethnic unrest without cracking down on Albanians which would be frowned upon by the rest of Europe.
Kosovo Albanians would get their own republic and there would be less pressure from the Macedonian Albanians for separate institutions.
The problem is how to kickstart the process without inflaming nationalist passions and international diplomatic arbitration is likely to be needed.

"Neither Serbia nor the Kosovo Albanians can propose talks lest the other side thinks its position is weakening or for fear of its own radicals. The same applies to Macedonia and the Albanians there," the diplomat said.

"All sides are loath to make concessions. But at the end of the day they have no choice but to accept what is actually the best solution. So it's up to the international community to put it forward to them."
